title: Literature and storytelling
objectives: Read a literary-style narrative excerpt and follow its devices
Recognize literary vocabulary and older forms, including po/opo in period dialogue
Retell a fable (pabula) or legend (alamat) with narrative connectors
Discuss language and culture using wika at kultura vocabulary

grammar.title: The narrator's toolkit: aspect and sequence in storytelling
grammar.explanation:
Tagalog narrative runs on the completed aspect for events and the incompleted for background: Umuulan nang gabing iyon (background) nang biglang kumatok ang isang estranghero (event) — 'It was raining that night when suddenly a stranger knocked.' Learn the pivots: nang 'when' (with your Unit 5 spelling mastered), noon 'then / at that time', biglang / bigla 'suddenly', samantala 'meanwhile' (Unit 4), maya-maya 'a little later', pagkalipas ng ilang taon 'after some years', at sa wakas 'and finally'.

Legends and fables have formulaic openers and closers. Openers: Noong unang panahon, ... 'Long ago...'; Sa isang malayong nayon, may nakatirang... 'In a distant village there lived...'. Closers: Mula noon, ... 'From then on...' — the signature of an alamat, which explains an origin: Mula noon, tinawag na Alamat ng Pinya ang kuwento. At iyan ang dahilan kung bakit... 'And that is why...'.

Dialogue inside narration uses the reporting frames you know (sabi ni, sagot ni, tanong ni) plus literary inversions: 'Saan ka pupunta?' ani Maria — ani/anya being the literary 'said'. Wika niya is another: 'literally 'his/her word (was)'.

grammar.title: Literary devices, and the language of respect in period settings
grammar.explanation:
The devices carry Tagalog names worth knowing because teachers and reviewers use them: tayutay 'figure of speech' as the umbrella; pagtutulad 'simile' (marked by parang, tulad ng, animo'y: Animo'y perlas ang mga luha niya — 'Her tears were like pearls'); pagwawangis 'metaphor' (no marker: Perlas ang kanyang mga luha); personipikasyon 'personification' (Humagulgol ang langit — 'The sky wept aloud'); pagmamalabis 'hyperbole' (Isang siglo kong hinintay ang sagot mo — 'I waited a century for your answer').

Period stories — set in the Spanish era or an idealized rural past — saturate their dialogue with respect language: children answer opo never oo, address elders with po in every sentence, and use kayo/ninyo/inyo even to parents, plus the honorifics Ka (Ka Pedro, for elders and comrades), Aling (Aling Rosa), Mang (Mang Tomas), and Don/Doña for landowners. The verb magmano / the phrase mano po marks the hand-to-forehead blessing. A modern character in fiction who says opo to parents signals traditional upbringing; one who says oo to a grandparent signals rudeness or modernity — writers exploit this contrast deliberately, and now you can read it.

grammar.title: Retelling: compressing a story aloud
grammar.explanation:
Retelling (muling pagsasalaysay) is a skill exam graders and dinner tables both prize. Structure your retelling in four beats. (1) Frame it: Ito ang alamat ng... / Isang pabula ito tungkol sa... (2) Set the scene with incompleted-aspect background: Noong unang panahon, may mag-inang nakatira sa tabi ng gubat... (3) Chain the events with completed verbs and sequence words: Isang araw, ... Pagkatapos, ... Dahil dito, ... Sa wakas, ... (4) Land the lesson or origin: Ang aral ng kuwento: ... / Kaya mula noon, ...

Keep the voice system working for you (Unit 1): keep the protagonist in the ang-slot so your listener never loses the thread. Compress dialogue into reported speech (Unit B1) unless a line is the punchline — punchlines stay direct: Sumigaw ang ina: 'Sana'y magkaroon ka ng isang libong mata!'

For discussing stories, arm yourself with: tauhan 'character', tagpuan 'setting', banghay 'plot', aral 'moral lesson', wakas 'ending', may akda 'author', katutubo 'indigenous/native', kuwentong-bayan 'folk tale'. Ang paborito kong tauhan ay... / Naganap ang kuwento sa... are your discussion frames.

example.en: Do you know the legend of the pineapple?

example.en: Grandmothers pass folk tales down to their grandchildren.

example.tl: Simple ang banghay pero malalim ang aral.

dialogue.title: Muling pagsasalaysay ng Alamat ng Pinya
dialogue.context: Liza practices retelling the Legend of the Pineapple to her language partner Paolo, who coaches her on storytelling technique.

lines.speaker: Paolo
lines.tl: Sige, subukan mo. Simulan mo sa tamang pambungad.
lines.en: Go on, try it. Start with the proper opener.

lines.speaker: Liza
lines.tl: Noong unang panahon, may mag-inang nakatira sa isang maliit na nayon: si Aling Rosa at ang kanyang anak na si Pina.
lines.en: Long ago, a mother and daughter lived in a small village: Aling Rosa and her daughter Pina.

lines.speaker: Paolo
lines.tl: Mahusay. Ilarawan mo si Pina — gumamit ka ng tayutay kung kaya mo.
lines.en: Good. Describe Pina — use a figure of speech if you can.

lines.speaker: Liza
lines.tl: Maganda si Pina, animo'y bulaklak sa umaga. Pero tamad siya, at laging may dahilan para hindi tumulong.
lines.en: Pina was beautiful, like a flower in the morning. But she was lazy, and always had an excuse not to help.

lines.speaker: Paolo
lines.tl: Pagtutulad iyang animo'y bulaklak, tama? O, ituloy mo. Anong nangyari nang magkasakit ang ina?
lines.en: That animo'y bulaklak is a simile, right? Go on. What happened when the mother fell ill?

lines.speaker: Liza
lines.tl: Isang araw, nilagnat si Aling Rosa. Inutusan niya si Pina na magluto ng lugaw. 'Opo, Inay,' sagot ni Pina, pero hindi niya mahanap ang sandok.
lines.en: One day, Aling Rosa came down with a fever. She told Pina to cook porridge. 'Yes, Mother,' Pina answered, but she couldn't find the ladle.

lines.speaker: Paolo
lines.tl: Pansinin mo: 'opo' ang sagot niya sa ina — ganyan ang mga anak sa mga lumang kuwento, kahit tamad.
lines.en: Notice: she answers her mother with 'opo' — that's how children are in the old stories, even lazy ones.

lines.speaker: Liza
lines.tl: Tapos, sa inis niya, sumigaw si Pina nang sumigaw na wala siyang makita. Sa sobrang galit ng ina, nasabi niya: 'Sana'y tubuan ka ng isang libong mata para makakita ka!'
lines.en: Then, in her irritation, Pina kept shouting that she couldn't find anything. In her great anger, the mother let slip: 'May you grow a thousand eyes so you can see!'

lines.speaker: Paolo
lines.tl: Ayan ang sumpa — laging may ganyang punto ang alamat. Tapos?
lines.en: There's the curse — legends always have that turn. And then?

lines.speaker: Liza
lines.tl: Maya-maya, naglaho si Pina. Pagkalipas ng ilang buwan, may tumubong kakaibang halaman sa bakuran: prutas na punong-puno ng mata. Mula noon, tinawag itong 'pinya', mula sa pangalang Pina.
lines.en: A little later, Pina vanished. After some months, a strange plant grew in the yard: a fruit covered in eyes. From then on, it was called 'pinya', from the name Pina.

lines.speaker: Paolo
lines.tl: Mahusay ang pagkakabuo mo — malinaw ang tagpuan, tauhan, at wakas. Ano ang aral?
lines.en: You built it well — setting, characters, and ending all clear. What's the lesson?

lines.speaker: Liza
lines.tl: Ang aral: ang katamaran ay may kapalit, at ang salitang binitawan sa galit ay hindi na maibabalik.
lines.en: The lesson: laziness has its price, and words released in anger can never be taken back.

reading.title: Ang Huling Habilin ni Ka Sela (isang bahagi)
reading.tl:
Umuulan nang gabing dumating si Andres sa lumang bahay ng kanyang lola sa nayon ng San Roque. Dalawampung taon siyang nawala sa lungsod; ngayon lamang siya nakabalik, at huli na — kinabukasan ang libing.

Sa may pintuan, sinalubong siya ng amoy ng lumang kahoy at ng kandila. Animo'y tumigil ang panahon sa loob ng bahay: naroon pa rin ang kahoy na bangko, ang banga ng tubig sa sulok, ang mga larawang naninilaw sa dingding. Sa gitna ng sala, sa puting kabaong, nakahimlay si Ka Sela.

"Kumain ka na ba, apo?" Iyon ang laging unang tanong ng lola niya noon, bago pa ang anumang kumustahan. Naalala niya ang sarili niyang sagot, paulit-ulit sa buong pagkabata: "Opo, Lola. Kabubusog ko lang po." Kahit hindi totoo. Alam iyon ni Ka Sela, at ipagluluto pa rin siya nito ng sinangag na may itlog.

Lumapit si Andres sa kabaong at nagmano sa malamig na kamay — ang kamay na nagturo sa kanyang magsulat, ang kamay na naghele sa kanya tuwing may bagyo. "Patawad po," bulong niya. "Dapat sana ay umuwi ako noon pa."

Maya-maya, may lumapit sa kanyang matandang babae na may hawak na maliit na kahon. "Ikaw si Andres, hindi ba? Ipinabibigay sa iyo ni Sela ito bago siya pumanaw." Sa loob ng kahon: isang lumang panulat, at isang liham na ang unang linya ay sapat na para pumatak ang kanyang mga luha: "Apo, kung binabasa mo ito, alam kong umuwi ka rin, sa wakas."
reading.en:
It was raining the night Andres arrived at his grandmother's old house in the village of San Roque. He had been away in the city for twenty years; only now had he returned, and he was late — the funeral was the next day.

At the doorway, the smell of old wood and candles met him. It was as if time had stopped inside the house: the wooden bench was still there, the water jar in the corner, the yellowing photographs on the wall. In the middle of the living room, in a white coffin, lay Ka Sela.

"Have you eaten, grandchild?" That was always his grandmother's first question back then, before any other greeting. He remembered his own answer, repeated throughout his childhood: "Yes, Grandmother. I've just eaten my fill." Even when it wasn't true. Ka Sela knew it, and she would cook him garlic rice with an egg anyway.

Andres approached the coffin and pressed the cold hand to his forehead — the hand that had taught him to write, the hand that had rocked him to sleep whenever there was a storm. "Forgive me," he whispered. "I should have come home long ago."

A little later, an old woman holding a small box approached him. "You are Andres, aren't you? Sela asked that this be given to you before she passed away." Inside the box: an old pen, and a letter whose first line was enough to bring down his tears: "Grandchild, if you are reading this, I know you finally came home, at last."

gloss.en: parting instruction, something entrusted before death
lulled, rocked to sleep (with a lullaby)
asked to be given (magpa- causative, incompleted)

exercises.prompt: Which is the classic opener of an alamat?
choices: Sa Kinauukulan:
Noong unang panahon,
Ayon sa ulat,
Una sa lahat,
exercises.explain: Noong unang panahon 'long ago / once upon a time' opens legends and folk tales. The others open letters, news reports, and speeches.

exercises.prompt: 'Animo'y perlas ang kanyang mga luha.' Which device is this?
choices: personipikasyon
pagtutulad (simile)
pagmamalabis (hyperbole)
headline grammar
exercises.explain: Animo'y is a literary simile marker like parang: 'her tears were LIKE pearls'. Without the marker (Perlas ang kanyang mga luha) it would be pagwawangis, metaphor.

exercises.hint: the one-syllable literary reporting word before a name
exercises.explain: Ani + name is the literary 'said': ani Lola 'said Grandmother'. With a pronoun it becomes anya 'said she/he'.

exercises.prompt: Sumayaw ang mga dahon sa hangin. Which device, and why?
choices: Personipikasyon — leaves are given the human act of dancing
Pagtutulad — the leaves are compared with 'parang'
Pagmamalabis — the number of leaves is exaggerated
Pagwawangis — the leaves are said to BE dancers
exercises.explain: Giving a human action (sumayaw 'danced') to non-human leaves is personification. No comparison marker, no exaggeration of degree.

exercises.prompt: ___ noon, tinawag na 'pinya' ang prutas na punong-puno ng mata. (From then on)
exercises.explain: Mula noon 'from then on' delivers the origin-explanation that every alamat builds toward.

exercises.tl: Noong unang panahon, may sakim na hari na nagnais angkinin ang lahat ng ginto sa kaharian.
choices: Long ago, a greedy king wanted to claim all the gold in the kingdom.
Recently, a generous king gave away all his gold.
Long ago, a poor king lost all his gold.
A king dreamed that his gold turned to stone.
exercises.explain: Sakim = 'greedy'; nagnais angkinin = 'desired to claim as his own'. The formulaic opener noong unang panahon plus a flawed ruler sets up a punishment tale.

exercises.prompt: Ang aral ng pabula: ang salitang binitawan sa galit ay hindi na maibabalik.
exercises.answer: The fable's lesson: words released in anger can never be taken back.
accept: The fable's lesson: words released in anger can never be taken back
The moral of the fable: a word let go in anger can no longer be returned
The lesson of the fable is that words spoken in anger cannot be taken back
exercises.explain: Aral is the moral; binitawan (from bitaw 'let go') is the released word; hindi na maibabalik = 'can no longer be brought back' — the abilitative ma- with i- root.

exercises.prompt: In a period story, a child answers her grandfather with 'Oo.' What is the writer most likely signaling?
choices: The child is exceptionally polite.
The child is being rude or marked as 'modern' — period norms demand 'opo'.
The grandfather is younger than the child.
Nothing; oo and opo are interchangeable in fiction.
exercises.explain: Period settings expect opo and po to elders without exception; a bare oo to a grandparent is a deliberate signal of rudeness or modern upbringing.

exercises.prompt: One day, the stranger knocked on the old woman's door and asked for water.
exercises.answer: Isang araw, kumatok ang estranghero sa pinto ng matandang babae at humingi ng tubig.
accept: Isang araw, kumatok ang estranghero sa pinto ng matandang babae at humingi ng tubig
Isang araw, kumatok ang estranghero sa pintuan ng matandang babae at humingi ng tubig
Isang araw, ang estranghero ay kumatok sa pinto ng matandang babae at humingi ng tubig
exercises.explain: Isang araw launches the event chain; completed verbs (kumatok, humingi) carry the narrative events, with the stranger held in the ang-slot across both.

exercises.prompt: From the reading: what does Andres do at the coffin?
choices: He places a pen inside it.
He presses his grandmother's hand to his forehead and asks forgiveness.
He reads a letter aloud to the mourners.
He lights a candle and leaves immediately.
exercises.explain: Nagmano sa malamig na kamay — the mano gesture of respect — then bulong niya: 'Patawad po. Dapat sana ay umuwi ako noon pa', the Unit 3 regret construction in action.

exercises.tl: Maya-maya, naglaho ang dalaga, at pagkalipas ng ilang buwan, may tumubong kakaibang halaman sa kanilang bakuran.
exercises.prompt: What happens in this part of the story?
choices: The young woman vanished, and months later a strange plant grew in their yard.
The young woman planted a garden that bloomed after a few months.
A strange plant vanished from the yard after a few months.
The young woman returned home carrying a strange plant.
exercises.explain: Naglaho = 'vanished'; pagkalipas ng ilang buwan = 'after some months'; tumubo = 'grew'. The vanish-then-transform sequence is the heart of many alamat.

exercises.prompt: It was as if time had stopped inside the old house.
exercises.answer: Animo'y tumigil ang panahon sa loob ng lumang bahay.
accept: Animo'y tumigil ang panahon sa loob ng lumang bahay
Parang tumigil ang panahon sa loob ng lumang bahay
Para bang tumigil ang oras sa loob ng lumang bahay
exercises.explain: Animo'y is the literary 'as if'; the everyday equivalent is parang. Both build the simile of stopped time — a line straight from the unit's reading.
